candidate.answerReason: Factoring P(x) − a at the four odd inputs forces both 9 and 105 to divide a, so 315 divides a. An explicit integer-coefficient polynomial attains a = 315.

methods.label: Factor the repeated values and attain the bound
methods.explanation:
The four equal values at odd inputs suggest subtracting \(a\), producing four known roots. First, \(a=P(1)\) is a positive integer because \(P\) has integer coefficients. Define
\[
G(x)=(x-1)(x-3)(x-5)(x-7).
\]
The factor theorem gives
\[
P(x)-a=G(x)R(x),
\]
where \(R\) also has integer coefficients. Indeed, dividing an integer-coefficient polynomial by a monic linear factor \(x-r\), with integer \(r\), leaves an integer-coefficient quotient; we can apply this successively at the four roots.

At \(x=4\), we have \(G(4)=9\), so
\[
-2a=9R(4).
\]
Since \(9\) is odd, \(9\mid a\). Similarly, \(G(8)=105\) gives \(105\mid a\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{lcm}(9,105)=3^2\cdot5\cdot7=315
\]
divides \(a\), proving \(a\ge315\).

We must also show that this bound can actually occur. Set \(a=315\) and seek \(P=315+GR\). At \(x=2,4,6,8\), the values of \(G\) are respectively \(-15,9,-15,105\). To make \(GR=-630\) at all four inputs, the required values of \(R\) are therefore
\[
42,\quad -70,\quad 42,\quad -6.
\]
The first and third values agree, suggesting the shift \(t=x-4\). The quadratic \(28t^2-70\) gives the required values at \(t=-2,0,2\). Adding a multiple of \(t(t^2-4)\) preserves these three values. At \(t=4\), the quadratic gives \(378\), while we need \(-6\); since \(4(4^2-4)=48\), the needed multiplier is \((-6-378)/48=-8\).

Thus take
\[
R(x)=28t^2-70-8t(t^2-4),\qquad t=x-4,
\]
and define
\[
P(x)=315+G(x)R(x).
\]
Both factors have integer coefficients. At the four odd inputs, \(G=0\), so \(P=315\). At the four even inputs, the prescribed values give \(GR=-630\), so \(P=-315\). This verifies every required value.

The smallest possible value is consequently \(\boxed{315}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
